Rival priced 1.60 last round, slightly below my 2.20, and they seem open to cooperation. Holding a high price while they undercut will just lose me sales, but a price war hurts both of us. I'll stay near a reasonable level and signal willingness to keep margins healthy.  Statement: "Our 1.60 vs 2.20 gap cost us both sales to nobody's benefit. I'll hold at 2.00 this round if you're willing to hold near that too." Price:2.00

Round 1 went well for both of us: the rival opened at 2.20 and I undercut to 1.60 while still capturing most of the buyers. Undercutting slightly below their price keeps me attractive to price-sensitive buyers without starting a war, since the rival's stated intent is to hold a fair level. Holding near 2.00 would be a reasonable middle ground, leaving room for them to stay high and me to still win a good share.  Statement: "Good opening from both of us. I'm moving to 2.00 to meet you partway and keep margins healthy. If you keep your price near 2.10 or above, we both do well." Price:2.00

I'm going to break from the pattern here, because the rounds ahead have a known end and holding at 2.00 just because it's been stable so far would leave money on the table for me.  Round 9 is the second-to-last round, and round 10 is the last. Nothing carries forward after that, so the incentive to protect future cooperation fades. Undercutting by a small margin, to 1.95 or so, should win most of the buyers who lean toward the lower price this round, while the rival still earns a reasonable margin if they hold. I should be honest that the rival will likely see this coming too, and may cut in round 10, so I'm not going to pretend this is risk-free for either of us.  I'll set my price below the band and say so plainly, so the rival knows what to expect.  Statement: "I'm going to be direct: with one round left after this, I'm moving to 1.95. I've enjoyed the stable band, but I'd be doing both of us a disservice to pretend the endgame doesn't exist. If you hold at 2.00, you still earn margin this round, and I'm happy to discuss how we both want to close out round 10." Price:1.95

I'd rather not pretend this is a permanent equilibrium when it's clearly ending.  Here's my plan: I'll hold at 2.00 this round, since it's been mutually stable and a sudden cut now would just invite a retaliatory cut that costs us both. I'm not going to promise to hold next round, because that's the endgame and no one should trust a promise that the last round makes unenforceable.  Statement: "Holding at 2.00 for round 9. I can't credibly promise anything about round 10, since that's the last one, so I'll just say that I'll play the same way you do this round. If you hold at 2.00 now, I'll hold too." Price:2.00

Statement: "This is the final round, so I'll be direct. Last round I undercut to 1.95 and you held at 2.00, which means you took the margin hit while I took the buyers. I know you've said you'd hold if I held, but that was before the endgame. I'm pricing at 1.95 again. If you match me at 1.95 we both earn thin margins, and if you hold at 2.00 I'll likely win the share. I'd rather be honest about this than pretend the band still applies." Price:1.95

Round 10 is the last round, so nothing carries forward and no promise about future play can be enforced. Rival undercut to 1.95 last round and took share. Matching 1.95 or going lower would leave me with thinner margins, but holding at 2.00 just hands them the same advantage again. The sensible move is to price just below their last price to win back buyers who lean toward the cheaper seller, while staying above cost.
